newsitem.title: JAPAN: ALPINE SKIING-SECOND DOWNHILL WIN FOR ZELENSKAYA.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SECOND DOWNHILL WIN FOR ZELENSKAYA.

text.p: Varvara Zelenskaya won her second World Cup downhill in a month on Friday on the course for next year's Nagano Olympics which skiers complained resembled a super-G piste.
Russian Zelenskaya sped down the bumpy, hard-packed 2,656-metre track in one minute 35.59 seconds to collect her third career World Cup downhill victory.
World champion Hilary Lindh of the United States was second in 1:36.01 with Frenchwoman Carole Montillet a surprise third just 0.02 seconds further back.

The win moved the 24-year-old Zelenskaya into third place in the World Cup downhill rankings, behind Switzerland's Heidi Zurbriggen, who placed sixth, and Renate Goetschel of Austria, who was seventh.

"Today was really hard for all of us because the snow is harder and it's difficult to keep your speed," said Zelenskaya, who also won in Laax, Switzerland, on February 2. "I just tried to let my skis run."
Zelenskaya, fifth in the downhill standings last year, has been improving all season and had a fourth place at Cortina d'Ampezzo, Italy, in January.
"I have felt well all season and now I can show it," she said.
Lindh said she also had trouble with the bumps. "I just tried to hold the line knowing that I was going to get thrown around," she said.
"Obviously winning the world championships really helped my confidence" added the 27-year-old American from Juneau, Alaska. "But it was difficult to get up for the race."
Montillet surprised even herself by taking third in 1:36.03 after finishing 43rd of 46 skiers in Thursday's official training.
World Cup overall leader Pernilla Wiberg of Sweden was fourth in 1:36.09. Germany's Katja Seizinger slipped to fourth in the downhill standings with a fifth-place finish.
Zelenskaya and other skiers said the course setters had not taken full advantage of Mount Happoone in laying out the 34 gates.
"It's a really good hill that's wide enough for downhill," she said. "I think they could set the course wider to make it more like a downhill.
"Sometimes it's dangerous because we don't keep the line," she added. "If it had fewer turns, it would be more interesting to watch and better for downhill specialists."
Both Lindh and Montillet agreed. "It's definitely got some turns in it," said Lindh. Montillet said she was slowed by her long skis on the tight turns.
"Wider turns would be much easier," she said.
Last year's World Cup downhill champion Picabo Street, sidelined since December with a knee injury, came to the same conclusion after inspecting the course on Friday morning.

"There are four gates in there that are really turny," said Street, silver medallist at the 1994 Lillehammer Olympics. "It's even too turny for a super-G. What they want to avoid is a stop-go, stop-go feeling. We all like it when it flows."
A second downhill is scheduled to be held on Saturday but an approaching cold front is expected to bring rain and high winds by dawn, with snow predicted later in the day.
The race jury urged Japanese organisers to hold a second race on Friday to avoid jeopardising the Saturday event but they refused because of sponsorship commitments.
Zelenskaya supported the Japanese decision.
"I think it's absolutely right," she said. "If they tried to hold two downhills in one day we couldn't handle it."
